matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: scheduled standards concepts for secure in-vehicle communications, metadata/debugging and network configuration
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Potential CAN XL communication and security configuration; SOME/IP metadata; and post-production E/E network configuration requirements, as described at concept level by AUTOSAR.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Planned concept-level capabilities for secure CAN XL communication, improved data collection/debugging, and flexible post-SOP PNC configuration; detailed final specifications and implementations were not inspected.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: AUTOSAR's roadmap and event page are authoritative for its own concept names/status and scheduled release event. Concept entries are not equivalent to published normative requirements, shipping implementations or broad deployment.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: AUTOSAR Concept Roadmap, R26-11 table: CONC 729.1 CANsec, CONC 737 SOME/IP Meta-Data and CONC 738 Dynamic PNC, lines 157-163; AUTOSAR Release Event 2026 page, lines 137-155, gives the R26-11 release event date of 2026-12-03.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Future/futuristic horizon relative to 2026-10-26: specifically scheduled concepts on the forthcoming R26-11 release roadmap. This is bounded to AUTOSAR's published roadmap, not a prediction of all future integration standards.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The release had not occurred by the review date. Roadmap descriptions are brief and no concept specification, implementation, conformance test, deployment, interoperability, security efficacy or regional adoption was assessed; schedule and scope may change.

relationship_context.explanation: The roadmap supplies forward-looking standards context for integration curricula and planning; the future concepts do not establish current prerequisites or a required architecture, and no learner sequence edge is inferred.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: An emerging automotive-software standards pathway now pairs the AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform's standardized service-oriented runtime and Classic-platform signal translation with CAPI 1.0, a common executable implementation and code generators released in August 2026. This moves beyond specification-only work for participating developers, but does not establish broad adoption or vehicle safety.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: automotive software-platform standard and common executable implementation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Adaptive applications, standardized functional-cluster services and interfaces, Classic-platform signals/control values, target ECU/hardware and implementation/code-generation environment.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Service-oriented application/runtime interfaces, Classic-to-Adaptive signal/service integration mechanisms, and a released common implementation/code-generator baseline for evaluation and development.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: AUTOSAR is authoritative for its own standard and release descriptions. CAPI is a newly released implementation initiative; statements about production use, collaboration and adoption are issuer-reported and not independently audited here.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform page, architecture and compatibility sections: standardized service interfaces, Signal-to-Service Translation, coexistence with Classic, and current R25-11 release; AUTOSAR CAPI 1.0 release notice dated 2026-08-20: executable base implementation, source code and code generators, lines 141-168.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Emerging standards/implementation development in automotive software integration as of 2026-10-26; the official issuer identifies a new common implementation, but current adoption and use remain independently unverified.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: AUTOSAR's published work is subject to copyright/IPR and commercial licensing terms; CAPI source access is described as available to partners. No implementation conformance, independent interoperability test, OEM-specific deployment verification, performance, cybersecurity assurance, safety certification or Nigerian adoption is established.

relationship_context.explanation: The Adaptive Platform specifies runtime services and integration boundaries, while CAPI supplies a common executable implementation path; the implementation can instantiate the platform but does not replace vehicle-specific integration, verification or safety evidence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: An established regulator-published ADS safety-method framework organizes design, testing and deployment considerations across system safety, ODD, OEDR, fallback/minimal-risk condition, validation, HMI, cybersecurity, crashworthiness, post-crash behavior, data recording, education/training and applicable laws; it encourages a self-documented process for assessment, testing and validation rather than prescribing one universal technical method.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: voluntary regulator safety-method framework and documented assessment/testing/validation process
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: ADS concept, intended ODD/OEDR and fallback behavior, safety/system design, HMI/cybersecurity/crashworthiness/post-crash requirements, test evidence, data recording and jurisdiction-specific laws.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: An entity-selected, documented approach describing safety considerations, assessment/testing/validation and optional public VSSA disclosure; NHTSA does not approve the VSSA.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: AV 2.0 is used as a U.S. voluntary framework for SAE levels 3-5; its 12 elements and self-documented assessment process are recommendations, not mandatory compliance criteria or a technical standard. The July 2026 draft-chapter initiative is not final guidance.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: NHTSA Automated Driving Systems 2.0: A Vision for Safety (2017), Executive Summary PDF pp. ii-iii and Section 1, ADS Safety Elements, PDF pp. 5-16; NHTSA Administrator SAE ATS keynote (2026-07-30), lines 75-80, confirms AV 2.0 remains current voluntary guidance while replacement draft chapters are developed.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established U.S. regulator guidance describing a broad safety process for SAE L3-L5 ADS; the 2017 framework is dated and the agency is soliciting draft replacement chapters as of July 2026.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The framework dates to 2017, is U.S.-specific and voluntary, and leaves organizations to select methods; it does not prove implementation quality, residual risk acceptability, safety-case sufficiency, regulator approval, current final guidance or Nigerian applicability. Draft replacement chapters on safety management, remote assistance and first responder interactions were not final at the July 2026 keynote.

relationship_context.explanation: The framework organizes safety topics and a documented lifecycle process that may structure methods such as scenario tests and validation; it does not replace technical standards, evidence validity, hazard-specific analysis or jurisdictional approval.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A foundational safety-V&V competency is recognizing that rare severe outcomes make direct road-exposure demonstrations statistically demanding: required miles depend on event rate, confidence/precision target and comparator assumptions, while underreporting and a moving human-driver benchmark add uncertainty. RAND's 2016 analysis concludes that driving alone cannot establish fatality/injury safety before release under its studied assumptions; it does not conclude that ADS safety is impossible to assess.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: statistical safety-evidence foundation and test-adequacy limitation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Event/failure definition and rate, exposure distance, desired confidence or precision, benchmark/comparator rate, reporting completeness and stated autonomy/ODD assumptions.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: An estimated exposure/sample requirement and an uncertainty-aware conclusion about what road-test data can establish under those assumptions; motivates combining evidence types rather than relying on road miles alone.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: RAND's numerical illustrations use U.S. historical human-driver data, rare-event statistical models, defined failure metrics and an explicitly scoped fully autonomous category; results change with vehicle class, ODD, comparator, event definition and assumptions.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Kalra and Paddock, RAND RR-1478-RC (2016), official 15-page report: Executive Summary pp. 1-2; statistical formulations/results pp. 3-6; benchmark and limitation discussion. Full official RAND PDF opened 2026-10-26; TRID bibliographic record cross-checked.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established foundational knowledge for planning ADS safety evidence and interpreting road-test claims; the report is a historical U.S. statistical analysis, not a current universal validation prescription.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: 2016 policy research, not a standard or regulator acceptance criterion. It does not establish today's crash rates, a universally required mileage threshold, scenario/simulator validity, causal safety improvement, or that simulation/other methods automatically solve residual uncertainty. U.S. rates and legal context do not transfer directly to Nigeria or other jurisdictions.

relationship_context.explanation: Road exposure contributes operational evidence but, under the report's rare-event assumptions, cannot alone supply timely pre-release statistical proof for severe outcomes; scenario, simulation, component and other evidence may complement it, but the report does not validate any particular substitute or fixed assurance sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Established vehicle-control design separates path stabilization from time-indexed trajectory tracking and includes geometric feedback, control-Lyapunov and feedback-linearization designs, plus predictive and linear-parameter-varying controllers; model class, reference type, stability conditions and computational burden differ across alternatives.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle-control method/design taxonomy and comparative assumption map
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle state/model, spatial path or time-indexed reference trajectory, controller design and tuning parameters, and computation budget.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Steering/control actions that stabilize path error or track a reference trajectory, with method-specific stability conditions and computation characteristics.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The survey's local stability and complexity statements hold under its stated kinematic/dynamic model, regularity, curvature, speed, horizon and discretization assumptions; they do not transfer automatically to arbitrary vehicles or ODDs.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Paden et al. (2016), Section V, especially V-A to V-D (PDF pp. 17-22): kinematic path stabilization, trajectory tracking, control-Lyapunov design, output-feedback linearization, predictive control and LPV controllers; Table II compares model/stability/complexity assumptions.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established urban-vehicle feedback-control design alternatives, scoped to the 2016 survey's methods and model assumptions; this does not characterize current production prevalence.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: A 2016 review of selected urban-vehicle control literature, not an exhaustive method inventory or production survey. Reported guarantees are model/condition-specific; it does not validate current software, full vehicle actuator limits, robustness across friction, degraded modes or public-road ADS safety.

relationship_context.explanation: The surveyed path-stabilization, trajectory-tracking, predictive and LPV designs address related reference-following tasks under different state models and assumptions; they are alternatives to assess for a stated vehicle/reference/constraint set, not interchangeable universal solutions or a required sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Emerging vehicle-control foundations include anticipating tire-road friction changes and understanding how friction-preview horizon and brake-actuator dynamics condition wheel-slip control; one 2024 ABS study reports experimentally validated simulation and prototype experiments, not a general ADS controller result.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: research-derived control foundation and actuator/friction-preview competency
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Wheel-slip/vehicle state, a previewed tire-road friction profile, prediction horizon and brake-actuator dynamic characteristics.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Wheel-slip control actions and braking response over a high-to-low friction transition; the record reports prototype real-time feasibility and performance improvement for its studied maneuvers.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The study's published abstract accurately summarizes its experimentally validated simulation and proof-of-concept electric-vehicle prototype experiments; no claim is made that preview information is available or necessary in all vehicles.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Tavolo et al. (2024), abstract and metadata in Politecnico di Torino IRIS institutional research record; DOI 10.1109/TIE.2023.3314917.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Emerging control-foundation knowledge for wheel-slip control under abrupt tire-road friction transitions; the reported system is ABS/NMPC, not lateral ADS trajectory tracking or a complete automated-driving stack.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Only the institutional repository record and abstract were inspected; the linked full paper was not opened in this pass. The study is ABS-specific and does not establish broad vehicle-control practice, production deployment, public-road ADS safety, universal friction sensing, or comparative superiority across vehicle/platform conditions.

relationship_context.explanation: When previewed friction is available to an ABS, its quality and horizon and brake-actuator dynamics condition the controller design; this is a conditional technical dependency, not a universal prerequisite or course sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Classical AV design decomposes route planning, behavior decision, motion planning and vehicle control; planners must account for environment structure, vehicle model and computational constraints.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: planning architecture taxonomy
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Mission goal, road/map representation, perceived scene, ego state, selected vehicle model and computational/operational constraints.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Route, behavior decision and motion path/trajectory as distinct planning artifacts; actuator commands belong to downstream feedback control.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Paden et al.'s urban-vehicle survey uses a modular conceptual decomposition and explicitly allows architecture partitions to vary; it does not assert one universal production stack.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Paden et al. (2016), Sections II-IV; see source-index entry D166-PADEN-PLANNING-CONTROL-SURVEY-2016.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Planning outputs a selected ego behavior/path/trajectory, not other-agent predictions or actuator commands.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Survey reflects its 2016 review scope and is not a present-day complete taxonomy or mandated order.

relationship_context.explanation: Vehicle/road geometry and state are inputs to the planning design; the paper describes model assumptions, not a universal training sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Current benchmark designs distinguish open-loop imitation from closed-loop evaluation; reactive-agent assumptions alter interaction and can alter planner rankings.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: benchmark evaluation design
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Logged sensor/scenario data, planner outputs, ego dynamics, selected non-ego traffic-agent model and evaluation metrics.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Open-loop prediction/planner metrics or closed-loop simulated behavior and score/rank under the benchmark's scenario and traffic assumptions.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: nuPlan and nuPlan-R define particular datasets, metrics and simulation setups; comparison results are conditional on those scenarios and agent models.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: nuPlan benchmark documentation metrics; nuPlan-R paper task and results, Sections III-IV (opened lines 63-67 and 149-183).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Planner candidate motion is evaluated under fixed logs or feedback simulation; the non-ego traffic model is an evaluation condition, not the planner itself.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Finite benchmark scenarios, simulators and a preprint; neither establishes on-road validity nor universal ranking changes.

relationship_context.explanation: Reactive multi-agent simulation complements closed-loop planning evaluation and challenges non-reactive/log-only metrics.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Autoware publishes a sequence of spatial/velocity/acceleration trajectory points and turn/hazard commands for downstream consumers; nuPlan supplies planner-specific metrics and scenario evaluation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: software interface and benchmark dataset/tool
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Planner map/route, ego state, sensed scene and planning configuration; benchmark scenarios and logged/simulated actor data.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Autoware trajectory-point sequence and associated planning commands; nuPlan scenario metrics and evaluation results.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The interface and metrics are specific to the documented Autoware and nuPlan versions; benchmark outputs are not vehicle-control actuation or road-safety evidence.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware Planning interface outputs; nuPlan official metrics page.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Explicit planner output contract and evaluation resource.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Autoware contract is version-specific; nuPlan metrics do not prove system-level safety.

relationship_context.explanation: The documented trajectory is consumed by the control component as its reference; this is a concrete interface handoff, not proof every stack has identical messages.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A selected behavior is converted into a feasible reference path/trajectory; feedback control tracks it and corrects execution error, so the planned motion and control command are separate outputs.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: planning-to-control output contract
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Selected ego behavior, road/obstacle constraints, vehicle state and trajectory-following feedback.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Planner reference path/trajectory, followed separately by controller-generated steering/acceleration/braking command.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The cited survey and Autoware describe this division in their architectures; implementations may fuse or repartition modules, so the handoff is not a universal organizational sequence.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Paden et al. (2016), decision hierarchy and Figure II.1, PDF pages 2-3, lines 183-248; Autoware Planning interface outputs.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Defines the planner output and downstream control context; it does not claim every architecture uses this exact hierarchy.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Paden is a 2016 urban-vehicle survey and Autoware is one maintained reference implementation; neither establishes a universal sequence or role assignment.

relationship_context.explanation: Both sources explicitly show a planning path/trajectory consumed as a reference by feedback control.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Learning-based reactive multi-agent traffic simulation is a research benchmark alternative to rule-based IDM and reports improved interaction diversity; diffusion/world-model approaches remain benchmark-specific evidence here.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: simulated traffic-agent method / benchmark component
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Benchmark scenario, agent observations/state, traffic-agent policy and simulator transition model.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Non-ego agent actions/trajectories and resulting closed-loop planner evaluation traces or metrics.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The reported diversity and planner comparisons are for nuPlan-R's trained/reactive-agent setup and evaluation scenes, not evidence of real-road behavior or universally superior agents.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: nuPlan-R abstract and Introduction, lines 3-17, 40-47.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: The learned method models surrounding traffic for planner evaluation; it is not itself evidence that an ego planner is learned or deployed.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Preprint, simulator and authors' reported metrics; no independent replication or operational safety claim.

relationship_context.explanation: Learned reactive agents are an alternative to rule-based IDM agents in the evaluation environment.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Scenario-based evaluation standards connect scenarios, requirements, ODD and test objectives; ISO 34502:2022 has limited-access-highway scope and ISO 34505:2025 is published for scenario-based ADS test-case generation and evaluation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: published scenario-evaluation standards
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Operational design domain, safety requirements, scenario descriptions and defined evaluation/test objectives.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Structured scenario-based evaluation and test-case generation/evaluation guidance.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: ISO 34502 scope and ISO 34505:2025 publication status are taken from current ISO catalogue records; neither record by itself establishes law, simulator validity or complete coverage.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: ISO 34502:2022 official abstract/status; current ISO 34505:2025 catalogue record; older DIS preview is superseded for publication-status claims.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Planning constraints and scenario evaluation are informed by ODD/test objective but standards do not specify a universal planner algorithm.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Standards are paid beyond preview; full normative text was not inspected. Verify applicability and jurisdictional adoption before compliance use.

relationship_context.explanation: They frame evaluation and ODD coverage, not planner implementation or legal approval by themselves.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Control design depends on vehicle-motion definitions/model and lateral/longitudinal dynamics; reference trajectory tracking is a separate functional responsibility from trajectory generation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle-dynamics terminology and control-function boundary
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle body/road coordinate conventions, motion state, speed, steering, tire/vehicle model and a reference path or trajectory.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Defined motion variables/model terms used to design feedback tracking and longitudinal/lateral control.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: ISO 8855 provides vehicle-dynamics vocabulary and Paden provides a historical architecture account; neither specifies one controller or complete modern ADS implementation.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: ISO 8855:2011 source-index record; Paden et al. Sections III-IV; Autoware Control Component design.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Vehicle-state/dynamics models support controller design; modeling detail varies with speed, maneuver, vehicle and ODD.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: ISO terminology is not a complete vehicle model or controller specification; no universal model fidelity is asserted.

relationship_context.explanation: A controller design needs a defined state/vehicle model and actuator behavior, though the sources do not prescribe one universal learning sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Maintained Autoware implementations document geometric pure-pursuit tracking, model-based MPC tracking, and a Smart MPC option using iLQR/MPPI with learned residual models; these illustrate alternatives and a hybrid extension, not a winner.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: controller algorithms and maintained software implementations
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Reference trajectory, estimated vehicle pose/velocity, vehicle model and configured tracking/actuation constraints; Smart MPC additionally uses its documented residual/model inputs.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Steering and/or longitudinal motion-control commands and controller diagnostics as defined by each implementation.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Documented Autoware packages and options are implementation examples; configuration, model and target platform determine behavior, and feature existence is not comparative safety validation.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware Trajectory Follower Nodes (controller options) and Smart MPC Trajectory Follower docs (iLQR/MPPI modes and residual adaptation).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Controllers consume vehicle state and a reference trajectory and emit control commands; learned residual dynamics augment rather than define the planner's target.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Project-specific implementations and configurations; no comparative performance or universal applicability follows. Smart MPC documentation records vehicle-specific degradation under model mismatch.

relationship_context.explanation: Pure pursuit and model-based MPC are controller alternatives for tracking; learned residual modeling is a hybrid extension documented in the separate Smart MPC package.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Research on learned residual/model components and risk-aware MPC/RL examines adaptation under vehicle-model uncertainty, while competition/racing conditions bound transfer claims.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: emerging control research methods
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle state/reference, model prediction error or learned residual data, risk/objective signals and racing or research scenario conditions.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Adapted model/controller parameters, candidate control actions or closed-loop racing trajectories, depending on the cited method.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Claims are limited to the distinct experiments and benchmarks in the cited papers; racing, competition and simulation evidence does not establish public-road ADS transfer or safety guarantees.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Indexed primary research cards for IAC feedback-linearized MPC and risk-aware RL racing, plus Autoware Smart MPC implementation notes.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: These are control/vehicle-dynamics methods, not general road-ADS production norms.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Research/competition settings; do not infer production prevalence, assurance or road transfer.

relationship_context.explanation: Learning can augment model-based control; evidence does not say it replaces state feedback, constraints or validation.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Autoware MPC documentation specifies vehicle model, state/path input and steering-command output; simulation/toolbox support can aid design and testing but is not deployment validation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: controller software, design toolbox and simulator
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle-model parameters, estimated state, reference path/trajectory, constraints and solver/configuration settings.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Steering or motion-control command, simulated/controller response and design-time test results.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Tool capabilities follow the named Autoware, MathWorks and CARLA documentation; a simulation/toolbox result does not demonstrate target ECU timing, hardware integration or road validity.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware MPC Lateral Controller design docs; MathWorks MPC Toolbox and CARLA simulator docs in the current source index.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Implementation tools support controller design and simulation at stated fidelity.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Tool docs establish features, not controller safety, plant fidelity or acceptance criteria.

relationship_context.explanation: Simulation and control-design toolchains complement algorithm implementation; hardware/vehicle evidence is still separate.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Autoware control outputs a motion control command based on a reference trajectory; the vehicle interface consumes it and converts normalized intent for platform-specific actuation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: planner/controller-to-vehicle-interface handoff
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Reference trajectory and current vehicle state at the controller; normalized motion command at the vehicle adapter.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Controller command delivered to the interface, then vehicle-specific actuation request and separately returned vehicle status.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The cited Autoware docs describe this software boundary; actual actuator mapping, limits, authority and timing depend on the vehicle-specific interface implementation.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware Trajectory Follower Nodes and Vehicle Interface tutorial/design documentation.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Controller output is distinct from actual vehicle state/status and from actuator electrical/mechanical outputs.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Reference architecture; vehicle interfaces and lower-level control differ across platforms.

relationship_context.explanation: The documented command is an input to vehicle adaptation, which converts it to specific vehicle command formats.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Integration requires consistent message semantics, units/frames, timestamps, communication and feedback status; control intent is not the same as measured actuation or mode.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle interface contract and timing/coordinate conventions
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Typed topic/service messages, coordinate-frame definitions, timestamped sensor/control values and vehicle-mode/status feedback.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Interpretable, time-associated and frame-consistent command/state exchanges across software components.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: ROS REP-103, IEEE 1588 and Autoware docs apply only to their stated conventions/interfaces; system-wide synchronization accuracy and safety are not inferred.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware Vehicle Interface design sections 2-4 and vehicle interface current message/API docs; ROS REP 103 and IEEE 1588 source-index records.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Interface contract and integration foundation, not planning/controller design.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Autoware and ROS examples are ecosystem-specific; IEEE 1588 is generic timing and does not guarantee achieved system accuracy.

relationship_context.explanation: Correct command/status interpretation presupposes compatible message, unit, frame and timing conventions; exact implementation varies.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Vehicle adapters may pass generalized steering/speed/acceleration commands or map them into vehicle-specific torque, voltage, pressure or pedal inputs, and translate platform status back to normalized messages.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: adapter design pattern and command/status translation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Normalized controller intent and platform-specific actuator/status signals.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Vehicle-targeted torque/steering/brake/throttle requests plus normalized measured state, control mode and diagnostics.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Autoware's vehicle-interface tutorial demonstrates possible adaptation paths, not a universal vehicle API, validated actuator limit, or guaranteed fault response.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware Vehicle Interface design and interface pages, sections Architecture, Features and Interface/Data Structure.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Explicit platform integration contract and adaptation alternatives.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: One maintained architecture; no universal CAN/Ethernet or actuator design is implied.

relationship_context.explanation: Direct generalized-command support and conversion through a vehicle-specific adapter are alternative integration patterns for differing vehicle capabilities.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: AUTOSAR Adaptive R25-11 lists services including communication, diagnostics, time synchronization, sensor interfaces, health management and update/configuration management for high-performance vehicle applications.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: automotive software platform and released architecture documentation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Application/service requirements, high-performance compute hardware and platform configuration.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Specified platform service interfaces and architecture for communication, diagnostics, time synchronization, health and related functions.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Claims refer to the named R25-11 release documentation; not every OEM adopts every service, nor do specifications prove a program's implementation or compliance.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform official page, Current Release and functional-cluster descriptions (opened 2026-10-24).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Platform middleware and vehicle integration context, not an autonomous driving application algorithm.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: No assertion all OEMs use AUTOSAR Adaptive; detailed specifications and commercial exploitation are subject to AUTOSAR terms.

relationship_context.explanation: Middleware can host/connect applications and services, but the page does not establish a required ADS dependency.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Vehicle interface emits vehicle-specific commands and returns velocity, steering, actuation and control-mode status; loss/unknown status is diagnosable and mode transition has latency.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle-interface output/status contract
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Normalized motion command, vehicle adapter feedback and timestamped mode/status signals.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Vehicle-specific actuation requests and returned velocity/steering/mode/diagnostic information, with timing relevant to integration checks.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The cited interface tutorial/PTP materials support software/status and time concepts; no numeric end-to-end bound, guaranteed fault detection or safe fallback is established.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware vehicle interface/control-mode docs; status page updated 2026-01-21.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Supports integration, system diagnosis and mode-feedback tasks; not safety case completion.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Autoware-specific design notes; no universal rates, latency budgets or safe response criteria.

relationship_context.explanation: Actual vehicle status feeds back to ADS components and informs whether autonomous/manual operation is active.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 address different risk causes: E/E malfunctions versus hazards from intended-function insufficiency/performance limits and reasonably foreseeable misuse; 21448 excludes 26262 faults and cybersecurity.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: functional-safety and SOTIF standards scope distinction
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Item/system definition, intended functions, hazards, malfunction behavior, performance limits and reasonably foreseeable misuse context.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Separate engineering processes and evidence for E/E malfunction-related risk and SOTIF-related insufficiency/misuse risk.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Claims are restricted to official public scope summaries; full licensed texts and program-specific editions were not inspected, and cybersecurity is not subsumed by ISO 21448.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: ISO 21448:2022 official scope/abstract (edition published June 2022; status to be revised as of 2025-10-14); ISO 26262 series source-index record.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Component/system functional safety and SOTIF are related but non-identical safety workstreams.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Standards are paid beyond preview and 21448 revision is underway; confirm edition/status and applicability before compliance decisions.

relationship_context.explanation: The standards address distinct hazard sources and can complement one another; neither alone is an ADS-wide safety case.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Scenario-based safety evaluation links scenario sets to requirements, ODD and test objectives; test-case generation and execution validity are explicit concerns, but simulation validity must be evaluated rather than presumed.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: scenario-based V&V methods and published test-case-generation standard
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: ODD, safety requirements, scenario parameterization, test objective and selected execution environment.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: benchmark, scenario exchange/tooling and published evaluation standard
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Logged/scenario data, actor/vehicle models, test parameters, evaluation metrics and execution configuration.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Reproducible benchmark scores/traces, scenario representations or virtual test results.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Repeatability is conditional on benchmark version, scenario selection, simulator and metrics; virtual results require separate validity/physical evidence and jurisdictional approval review.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: nuPlan Planning Benchmark documentation; ISO 34502:2022, ISO 34505:2025 and ISO/PAS 34506:2026 catalogue records; ASAM OSI/Scenario source-index records.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: ISO/PAS 34506:2026 qualifies a virtual test environment, but explicitly does not assess individual simulator-model accuracy or ADS performance. Simulator models, scenario distributions, sensor/vehicle fidelity and coverage still limit inference; no qualification implies road performance.

relationship_context.explanation: Virtual testing complements but does not replace closed-course, on-road, system-level and approval evidence.

matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Regulatory/approval context is jurisdiction-, vehicle- and use-case-specific; distinguish guidance, regulation, draft and voluntary disclosure.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Safety V&V work outputs include requirements-linked test plans/results, scenario and ODD coverage, evidence for safety arguments and approval dossiers; employer postings document such tasks conditionally for ADS QA, integration and homologation assignments.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: conditional employer role-task evidence and V&V work products
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Requirements, test objectives, ADS feature/ODD, scenario suites, test results and jurisdiction/program dossier criteria.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Established trajectory-tracking techniques include geometric path followers (for example Pure Pursuit/Stanley), feedback control (PID), optimal/state-feedback methods (LQR) and model-predictive control; the selected model fidelity and controller depend on speed, lateral dynamics, vehicle characteristics and computational limits. Path tracking is spatial, whereas trajectory tracking follows a time-indexed reference.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: lateral controller families and comparative research study
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Spatial path or time-indexed trajectory, vehicle state, vehicle model, controller parameters and maneuver/test conditions.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Steering/lateral control action and tracking, stability and comfort measures; Artuñedo et al. compares five controllers in simulation and instrumented-vehicle tests.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Controller behavior and ranking are conditional on model, vehicle, tested trajectories, tuning method and metrics; path tracking is not identical to timed trajectory tracking.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Artuñedo et al. (2024), full arXiv-hosted journal PDF, Sections 1 and 5-7: controller set, common tuning/evaluation design and instrumented-vehicle test boundary; 2026 Annual Reviews in Control systematic review, official publisher-indexed abstract and substantial Sections 2-8 text for path-versus-trajectory definitions and review scope; Paden et al. (2016) as historical cross-check.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: This is the classical control-method foundation for vehicle-control work; it follows vehicle-state/dynamics and reference-path/trajectory concepts and does not include trajectory generation itself.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The complete 2026 Elsevier review text was inspected via a third-party copy whose uploader provenance is unverified; publisher/institution metadata matches the copy. It is a secondary review, not a primary comparative experiment, and its cross-study comparisons use heterogeneous setups/metrics. The 2024 Artuñedo study is a separate, scoped lateral-controller comparison, not a field-prevalence study or universal ranking, and its results do not generalize automatically to other vehicles, maneuvers or ADS safety.

relationship_context.explanation: Geometric, PID, LQR and MPC controllers are method families with differing model, state, constraint and compute needs. A selected controller consumes a reference and vehicle state; its commands are evaluated against tracking, stability and feasibility objectives.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Safety-oriented MPC literature is grouped in the inspected 2025 author preprint into collision/risk mitigation, trajectory tracking/path following, and intersection/coordination, with nonlinear, robust, adaptive and learning-enhanced variants; the preprint itself flags scalability and computational-efficiency challenges. The later 2026 journal review's broader 101-study synthesis is visible only in publisher-indexed excerpts.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: systematic-review taxonomy of safety-control methods and validation limitations
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Peer-reviewed AV MPC studies screened under the review's stated safety objectives, period, search and inclusion criteria.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Qualitative method/application categories and reported evidence/limitation themes; the earlier manuscript and 2026 journal article are treated as distinct versions.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The 2025 manuscript is not peer reviewed and has internal count discrepancies; do not transfer the 2026 journal study count to it or treat either synthesis as direct safety proof.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Mahmood and Szabolcsi, Preprints.org v1 (2025), Abstract and Sections 2-3, full page opened; compare with Automation 2026, 7(3), 88 official publisher-indexed Abstract, Sections 2-6 and Table 5 excerpts. Do not transfer study totals between versions.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: This provides a bounded map of contemporary safety-control technique families and validation caveats. It links safety V&V to planning/control evidence without turning any controller into a safety case or approval result.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The 2026 publisher-indexed article text is extensive but not a complete independently inspected article. The 2025 source is an earlier non-peer-reviewed manuscript with internally differing study totals and is not equivalent to the version of record. Neither qualitative review provides independent efficacy evidence or establishes road-deployment safety.

relationship_context.explanation: Safety-oriented MPC formulations complement system-level safety analysis and scenario/physical V&V; simulation results require validity, uncertainty and computational-feasibility checks before supporting operational claims.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A current research taxonomy contrasts modular pipeline planning, with explicit route/behavior/trajectory interfaces, against end-to-end learned mappings from perception inputs toward trajectory or control outputs; the tradeoff includes traceability and fault localization versus learned integration/generalization challenges.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Teng et al. (2023), arXiv:2303.09824, Introduction I-A to I-D (HTML lines 17-38) and challenges/future perspectives (lines 61-96).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: This is a method/design taxonomy at the planning system boundary; end-to-end scope can include perception and control, so outputs differ from a modular ego planner.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Survey manuscript and incomplete algorithm-section extraction; it reports a research taxonomy, not universal industry prevalence, deployed performance or superiority. No detailed comparison of constituent planner algorithms is inferred.

relationship_context.explanation: The two designs can address driving decision/trajectory generation under different modularity and observability assumptions; end-to-end papers may output controls rather than a planner trajectory, so compare only when task/output contracts match.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: method/design taxonomy
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Modular design uses upstream perception, localization, map/route, vehicle state and constraints; end-to-end designs may take raw or encoded sensor inputs.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Modular route/behavior/trajectory artifacts; end-to-end trajectory points or control commands depending on the design.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The survey's pipeline/end-to-end distinction is used as an architecture-level comparison, not as a statement that all end-to-end systems span the whole stack.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Established motion-planning technique families include graph search, sampling/tree exploration and variational optimization; a trajectory candidate must be judged against the selected vehicle model, feasibility limits and task objective rather than by planner-family label alone.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Paden et al. (2016), Sections IV-A to IV-C and vehicle/control model assumptions in Sections II-III; CommonRoad Tutorial 2 scenario constraints at page lines 14-21.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Algorithms search/optimize an ego route/path/trajectory through an environment and vehicle model; they do not predict other-agent intent by definition.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Paden is a 2016 urban-vehicle survey and the CommonRoad tutorial is one benchmark case; examples do not rank families or establish performance across ODDs.

relationship_context.explanation: Search, sampling and optimization are alternative planning mechanisms when tasked with the same feasible path/trajectory output; they differ in representation, constraints, search budget and solution guarantees.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: algorithm families
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Road/obstacle representation, start/goal or behavior target, ego state and a vehicle/dynamics feasibility model.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Candidate or selected path/trajectory, with feasibility/cost checks defined by implementation.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The method assumes a defined planning problem and environment model; interaction forecasts and safety validation may be separate components.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Input-constrained control barrier functions are a current research technique for enforcing state-safety conditions while respecting vehicle input limits; an inspected automobile study demonstrates a viability-kernel human-assist design in simulation, not a production ADS safety filter.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Tezuka et al. (2025), JRM 37(5), publisher abstract lines 28-51: four-wheel model, viability kernel, state and input constraints, minimal intervention, simulation-only validation.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Control-side technique constrains a controller's admissible action to preserve a specified safe set; it does not generate the reference trajectory.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Abstract-level access only; human-assist context and simulation validation limit direct transfer to autonomous driving, roadway safety or certification.

relationship_context.explanation: A safety filter can constrain a nominal tracking/assist command when the safe set, vehicle model and input authority are specified; this study does not show a universal controller integration contract.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: control algorithm / safety-filter method
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle state, reference/control request, modeled safe set, vehicle model and actuator/input bounds.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: An admissible control/assist action constrained by the designed barrier and input limits.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Model, viability-set and actuator constraints used by the paper; state constraints and simulation scenario are not general road guarantees.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform R25-11 is the listed current release on the official platform page; its published architecture/design documents specify service areas including communication, diagnostics, time synchronization, security and platform health, but adoption is OEM- and program-specific.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform current release page; R25-11 Explanation of Adaptive Platform Software Architecture, PDF pages 0-1 (release/status) and functional-cluster sections; Explanation of Adaptive Platform Design, PDF pages 0-1 and diagnostics/time synchronization chapters.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Standards/platform architecture context for integration engineers; these specifications do not define the complete vehicle interface or a universal ADS architecture.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: AUTOSAR documents are subject to stated information-use/IPR and commercial-use terms; confirming the standard release does not prove any OEM adoption, implementation conformance or safety certification.

relationship_context.explanation: The platform's standards and explanatory documents guide possible integration designs; using this platform is not a prerequisite for all vehicle integration roles or systems.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: platform standard and official learning/reference documentation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Vehicle software architecture, service/client requirements, network and deployment context for the target vehicle program.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Specified platform services and interfaces for communication, diagnostics, time synchronization, security and health management.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The target program selects and licenses/adopts AUTOSAR Adaptive; R25-11 scope is not projected to other platform versions or OEM implementations.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A 2026 research method evaluates scenario-set coverage across attribute ranges, ODD/behavior competencies, out-of-ODD cases and road-rule compliance, demonstrated on an ALKS case study; it is a proposed coverage analysis technique, not proof that a test set or ADS is safe.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Chodowiec et al. (2026), IEEE Access 14, pp. 33117-33139; full PDF abstract and introduction, pages 0-2, lines 12-30 and 57-122; full paper methods/results in accessed PDF.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Technique analyzes scenario-set coverage relative to a specified system ODD and behavior competency; separate from generating the planner or executing physical tests.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: One peer-reviewed framework and ALKS case study; coverage dimensions do not prove exhaustive rare-event coverage, simulator validity, road performance or applicability to Nigerian traffic rules.

relationship_context.explanation: Coverage analysis complements scenario generation and test execution by checking represented ranges and ODD/behavior dimensions; physical/on-road validation and an overall safety argument remain separate.

matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: scenario coverage analysis technique
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Declared ODD attributes, behavioral competencies, scenario set, scenario-rule associations and the analysis framework.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Coverage metrics and identified gaps for scenario attribute ranges, ODD/behavior competency, out-of-ODD response and road-rule compliance.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The ODD, behavior competencies, rule set and scenario parameterization are specified adequately for the chosen ALKS-like study context.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Established ECU integration separates application software from hardware-oriented services through AUTOSAR Classic's RTE/basic-software architecture, while UDS defines data-link-independent client/server diagnostic services for ECUs; current AUTOSAR records retain this diagnostic family alongside newer platform APIs.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: automotive software architecture and diagnostic communication standard
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: ECU software components, configured RTE/basic-software interfaces, diagnostic tester requests, ECU diagnostic data and functions, and project-specific network/transport configuration.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Component communication and hardware abstraction across ECU layers; UDS diagnostic service requests/responses for data, fault information and controlled routines/actuators.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: AUTOSAR Classic is a standards architecture example, not a claim that every vehicle uses AUTOSAR. ISO 14229-1:2026 is the current published UDS edition; its catalogue abstract is used for diagnostic scope, not detailed service conformance. Historical relevance is grounded in AUTOSAR release history rather than treating the 2026 edition as itself historical.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: AUTOSAR Classic Platform official overview: architecture and methodology sections; AUTOSAR history: Classic releases from 2005 onward; ISO 14229-1:2026 catalogue, abstract and publication status.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established ECU abstraction/diagnostics layer of system integration, not AV planning/control logic or a complete in-vehicle network design.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The public AUTOSAR pages summarize architecture and release dates; ISO abstracts do not provide full licensed requirements. UDS specifies diagnostic communication services, not ordinary ECU-to-ECU traffic or implementation requirements. No market prevalence, conformance, cybersecurity assurance or Nigerian adoption is claimed.

relationship_context.explanation: Platform and diagnostic interface contracts are prerequisites for integrating and servicing ECU software in a configured vehicle network; they do not dictate a universal software architecture or learning sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Current vehicle-interface implementations adapt generic acceleration and steering targets into vehicle-specific actuation using calibrated command maps and feedback, instrument command-to-publish latency, and expose mode/fault state; an Apollo Devkit example gates auto engagement on actuator response and transitions to a configured emergency mode for selected faults.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle-specific command adaptation and interface fault-handling techniques
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Target acceleration, velocity and steering angle; measured speed/odometry and steering/actuation feedback where configured; vehicle-specific calibration data; actuator response, CAN/chassis status and current operating mode.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Vehicle-specific throttle/brake and steering commands; normalized vehicle/actuation status; command-to-publish timing diagnostics; mode/error state and configured emergency transition/commands for selected faults.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Command maps and steering-ratio parameters are calibrated for the exact vehicle/interface and operating configuration. Apollo's watchdog and emergency actions are only the checked-in Devkit example; no behavior is generalized to other vehicles. Interface timestamps and reported status are assumed valid for the implementation under test.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware raw_vehicle_cmd_converter documentation, Overview/reference-data/Vehicle Adaptor/Latency Measurement sections (lines 1082-1123); Apollo Chassis schema, DrivingMode/ErrorCode and status/timestamp fields (lines 731-875); Apollo Devkit controller, EnableAutoMode response checks and SecurityDogThreadFunc fault transition (lines 2971-3033 and 3558-3684).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Current software-to-vehicle interface integration at the actuation boundary: generic controller targets are converted to a particular drive-by-wire interface and accompanied by vehicle status/mode/fault reporting; this is distinct from trajectory tracking algorithm design and from a system safety case.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Project documentation/code does not establish vehicle deployment, safety certification or universal practice. Autoware's latency metric ends at software publication, not measured physical actuation. Its vehicle-adaptor feature is labeled under development. Apollo fault thresholds and emergency commands are platform-specific; no safe-stop efficacy, timing guarantee, or independent validation is shown.

relationship_context.explanation: Command adaptation complements the trajectory controller by translating its desired acceleration/steering into vehicle-specific signals and returning state/diagnostics. Interface-level fault handling consumes platform feedback; it does not replace the vehicle safety concept, independent fallback validation, or controller stability analysis.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: The ASAM archive documents an established HIL/XIL test-automation interface lineage: HIL V1.0.0 in 2009, followed by XIL releases through V2.2.0 in 2020. This is evidence of a versioned testbench-interface standard family, not proof of ADS-specific adoption or safety effectiveness.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: historical test-automation and generic simulator interface standard family
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Test-automation tooling, test cases/signals and a compatible model, software, hardware or vehicle test bench configured for the particular interface release.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Versioned HIL/XIL interface specifications and associated testbench integration references enabling automation tooling to communicate with compatible benches; release chronology only is claimed for the historical editions.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The ASAM archive's release dates and labels correctly identify prior editions. The current page is used only to clarify the standard family's scope as an interface API, not to project current 3.0.0 features backward onto earlier editions.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: ASAM XIL - Previous Releases archive, lines 145-219 (HIL V1.0.0, 22 June 2009; XIL V2.0.0-2.2.0, 2013-2020); current ASAM XIL datasheet/overview, lines 145-200, defining the Generic Simulator Interface and its test-automation/MIL-SIL-HIL scope.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established/traditional testbench interface lineage for hardware/software/model-in-the-loop automation; this is the historical standard/tool-interface context, not an ADS simulator, dataset or safety validation result.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Release listings do not prove implementation prevalence, ADS-specific use, conformance, simulator fidelity, scenario coverage or safety effectiveness. Full historical specifications and actual deployment were not inspected; member access/pricing terms are not evidence of public implementation.

relationship_context.explanation: A testbench API complements simulators, ECUs and test automation by defining an interface boundary; it does not itself supply the simulator, test scenarios, validity evidence or safety argument.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Traditional CAN CC integration separates data-link/physical-layer responsibilities from higher-layer services: CAN frames carry content identifiers that arbitrate bus access, while ISO 15765-5 specifies an OSI-layered DoCAN connection from external diagnostic equipment through a vehicle DLC to a CAN network.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: in-vehicle CAN communication and diagnostic-layer foundation
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: CAN data-link frames from network nodes, message identifiers, physical bus signaling, and external diagnostic equipment connected through a vehicle DLC.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Arbitrated CAN CC frame access with error detection/fault confinement, plus an ISO 15765-5 DoCAN communication path across OSI layers 1-4 between external diagnostic equipment and the CAN network.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The CiA summary is used for protocol behavior; ISO catalogue/OBP records establish publication identity and scope, not all normative details. ISO 15765-5's external-diagnostic path does not imply every vehicle uses this configuration.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: CiA CAN CC knowledge page sections 'CAN data link layer' and 'Error detection and fault confinement'; ISO 11898-1:2024 catalogue scope; ISO 15765-5:2023 OBP sections 1 and 5, especially OSI layers and DLC-to-CAN connection.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established/traditional CAN CC and DoCAN foundation retained in current standards catalogues; this is a layered vehicle-network/diagnostic interface example, not the complete contemporary vehicle network stack.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: No timing determinism, deadline guarantee, security/authentication, safety integrity, deployment prevalence or universal architecture is inferred. ISO 11898-1:2024 includes CAN CC/FD/XL options; this claim is deliberately limited to CAN CC and DoCAN framing.

relationship_context.explanation: Vehicle command and diagnostic semantics depend on lower-layer network transport and physical connectivity; the standards define distinct layers and do not supply the application contract or vehicle-specific safety behavior.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Foundational urban-vehicle planning literature distinguishes graph/search, sampling-based and trajectory-optimization approaches; their suitability depends on map/environment structure, vehicle-state constraints and the planning horizon, not a universal ranking or mandatory serial stack.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: historical planning-method design taxonomy
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Mission or maneuver objective, map or sensed free-space representation, vehicle state/model and kinematic/dynamic feasibility constraints.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: A route, feasible geometric path or time-parameterized trajectory candidate, depending on the planning level and method.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Paden et al.'s 2016 survey is treated as a review of established urban-vehicle method families, not a current prevalence census; graph/search, sampling/tree and variational optimization solve related but not identical problem formulations.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Paden et al. (2016), Sections II-IV, full 27-page PDF; Section IV method-family survey. MIT DARPA Urban Challenge Development Plan (2006), Section 2.3, pp. 6-7, used as contextual counter-search only for the distinction between route-level mission planning and kinodynamic local planning.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established/traditional planning design alternatives; method choice depends on environment representation, vehicle constraints and planning scope, and does not prescribe a universal component ordering.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: A 2016 survey taxonomy does not establish which methods dominate current production, compare all implementations under common metrics, prove a universally superior method or establish road safety. The MIT document is a proposal, not proof of completed system implementation.

relationship_context.explanation: Graph/search, sampling and optimization are alternative or combined design families for route/path/trajectory problems under distinct representations and constraints; the sources do not make them interchangeable in every scenario or a required learning sequence.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A 2008 Stanford field report documents an actual historical autonomous-driving software implementation used in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge: distributed planning/navigation modules included global dynamic programming, road-navigation trajectory rollouts and a hybrid-A* planner, alongside a vehicle controller and drive-by-wire interface.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: historical integrated autonomous-driving planning software implementation case
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: DARPA RNDF route network, mission checkpoints, local map/obstacle data and vehicle state.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Global cost-to-go/path guidance, locally simulated candidate trajectories and hybrid-A* path plans made available to the vehicle controller; the report identifies the actual planner/controller processes.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The system authors' peer-reviewed field report is primary evidence for the described Junior implementation and event, not for broader industry prevalence.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Montemerlo et al. (2008), Sections 3 and Table 1, PDF pp. 3-4 (software pipeline and actual race processes); Sections 6.1-6.3, PDF pp. 13-18 (global DP, RNDF road navigation and hybrid A*).
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Established/traditional historical planning software case, limited to an integrated prototype for the staged 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge ODD.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: The article documents but does not release the complete software or RNDF dataset. The staged competition had a constrained U.S. urban ODD and speed limits; it is not evidence of present-day public-road safety, production deployment or regulatory approval.

relationship_context.explanation: The report's planner methods are realized in an integrated software pipeline with separate vehicle-control and drive-by-wire modules; this is one historical implementation, not a universal architecture.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: In Stanford's 2007 Urban Challenge system, global dynamic programming on the RNDF generated expected-time/risk cost-to-go for route choices, while a local planner evaluated vehicle-simulated lane trajectories or a hybrid-A* free-form path; these path/trajectory products were distinct from the downstream low-level steering/throttle/brake control.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: historical planning output and planner-to-controller handoff
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Mission checkpoint, discretized RNDF, local obstacles/free-space, vehicle state and candidate control/trajectory simulations.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Route-level cost-to-go and selected path/trajectory for the controller; steering, throttle and brake commands are produced downstream by the vehicle controller, not by the planning output itself.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The claim describes the hierarchy documented by the Junior authors, where global route selection informs local road navigation and free-form planning; parking and road navigation use different planners.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Montemerlo et al. (2008), Sections 6.1-6.3, PDF pp. 13-18, especially dynamic-programming cost-to-go (pp. 13-14), local trajectory evaluation (p. 14), hybrid-A* output (pp. 15-18); Section 3/Table 1, PDF pp. 3-4, names PLANNER and CONTROLLER processes.
matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Historical route/path/trajectory handoff and downstream role boundary in one competition system, not a current standard interface or general production stack.
matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Competition-specific implementation and map assumptions; not a normative message contract, general role requirement, public-road safety proof or current product architecture. Reported failure conditions include inability of the road-navigation planner to handle blocked roads/intersections and incompleteness of hybrid A*.

relationship_context.explanation: The global RNDF cost-to-go informs local path/trajectory selection; the selected motion plan is consumed by a separate low-level controller, which generates actuator commands.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Current ADS planning foundations include treating the operational design domain as explicit where/when capability limits and recognizing that interactive maneuvers such as merges and unprotected turns may require joint multi-agent motion forecasts rather than isolated per-object prediction; the applicable ODD and evidence remain system- and jurisdiction-specific.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: ODD and interactive-prediction planning competency
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Roadway/geographic/speed/environmental operating limits, map and ego state, and relevant other-agent histories or forecasts in interactive maneuvers.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: An ego behavior/path/trajectory decision conditioned on the declared operating limits and interaction-relevant agent hypotheses, with validation scope tied to the prescribed ODD.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: Waymo's paper establishes a research-data and forecasting need for joint predictions in interactive examples, while NHTSA describes an ODD framework and voluntary U.S. practices; neither requires one specific planner architecture.

relationship_context.explanation: The planner's intended operating limits constrain the behavior it should select and validate; in interactive maneuvers, other-agent motion hypotheses may condition ego behavior. These dependencies do not require a separate predictor module or define a universal learning order.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Emerging research increasingly couples multi-agent behavior prediction with ego planning; the NeurIPS 2024 BeTop study proposes topological joint-behavior representations and contingency learning to guide interactive trajectory generation, but reports benchmark evidence rather than deployed-road validation.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: NAVSIM is an emerging data-driven benchmark/tool that computes short-horizon BEV simulation metrics from logged real-world scenes without reacting other agents to the evaluated policy; its authors report better alignment with closed-loop scores than traditional displacement errors, while explicitly noting simulator domain gap and non-reactive limits.

matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Logged sensor scenes and policy trajectory outputs over a selected short horizon, OpenScene/nuScenes-derived data, and BEV scene abstractions.

relationship_context.explanation: NAVSIM's log-based non-reactive evaluation can complement reactive closed-loop simulation by scaling data-driven comparisons; neither substitutes for physical/on-road validation or proves a planner ranking outside its protocol.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A bounded CommonRoad 2023 competition report compares two materially different current motion-planning designs under shared interactive scenarios and compute limits: reachability-based decision-making plus optimization, and trajectory sampling/evaluation. matrix_claim_mappings.claim: Current vehicle-control foundations require accounting for coupled lateral/longitudinal motion, speed-dependent and time-varying parameters, tire-road adherence and actuator dynamics; the dynamic bicycle/single-track model is a useful reduced model, but linear controller designs rely on stated small-slip, linear-tire, constant-friction and constant-speed assumptions.

matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The reduced single-track model simplifies real dynamics; its linearized form assumes small sideslip, tires in the linear force-slip region, constant road friction and constant longitudinal speed. relationship_context.explanation: Model fidelity, vehicle-state inputs and actuator assumptions condition tracking design and constraint validity; these are technical dependencies, not a prescribed curriculum order or universal model choice.

matrix_claim_mappings.area_context: Current publicly listed international standards relevant to safety engineering and evaluation of vehicle-control functions; status is that of catalogued editions, not national law.

matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Safety-related properties usable to construct a safety-assurance claim concerning unreasonable risk, subject to complete normative requirements and project-specific evidence.

matrix_claim_mappings.locator: ISO/PAS 8800:2024 official catalogue abstract: https://www.iso.org/standard/83303.html; scope and exclusions inspected 2026-10-27.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Public catalogue abstract only; full PAS text, implementation evidence, national adoption and regulator acceptance not reviewed. relationship_context.explanation: AI safety properties complement functional-safety, SOTIF, ADS scenario evaluation and system-level V&V; the PAS abstract does not replace these or establish a complete safety case.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: An archived Autoware.Auto vehicle-interface reference specifies timestamped normalized acceleration/steering commands, vehicle-state commands, odometry/status feedback, and concrete command-handling behaviors: map normalized inputs to actuators, hold commands between updates, reject unsafe commands or sequences, fall back to a stop after command timeout, and allow manual override. These are bounded interface techniques in one project reference design, not universal vehicle-interface requirements.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: vehicle-interface command-handling and fallback technique set
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: Timestamped normalized longitudinal acceleration and front/rear wheel-angle requests; discrete vehicle-state commands; incoming vehicle state and platform-specific actuator mapping.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: Platform-specific actuation; state and odometry reports; held command between updates; rejection of unsafe command sequences; timeout-triggered stop behavior; manual override response.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The implementation is a vehicle-interface component for a sufficiently compatible Autoware.Auto-derived stack, and the vehicle supports the command/status contract. Vehicle-specific mappings, validated safe-stop dynamics and timing thresholds must be supplied and verified separately.
matrix_claim_mappings.locator: Autoware.Auto Vehicle-Interface-Reference-Implementation, Scope and Reference Implementation, lines 22-33; timestamped control-command schema and rationale, lines 40-68; output/state-report contract, lines 144-174 and 237-252; Behaviors, lines 253-263 and linked sections Command mapping, Zero order hold, Unsafe Command Rejection, Timeout Fallback Behavior and Manual Override.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim: A 2026 autonomous-racing study reports a hierarchical control design combining high-level feedback-linearized MPC with low-level model-based yaw-rate and powertrain-based acceleration controllers. Its reduced-order prediction model explicitly accounts for steady-state lateral slip, and the abstract reports full-scale IAC AV-24 track implementation and experimental testing. This is a specific high-speed racing design, not a general road-ADS controller recommendation.
matrix_claim_mappings.item_type: hierarchical reduced-order feedback-linearized MPC and vehicle-control method
matrix_claim_mappings.inputs: The publisher abstract describes reference-trajectory tracking and vehicle-dynamics prediction; detailed state, sensor, constraint and actuator interfaces are not treated as verified from the blocked full text.
matrix_claim_mappings.outputs: High-level yaw-rate/longitudinal-acceleration control targets from FBL-MPC and low-level yaw-rate/powertrain acceleration commands, as summarized in the publisher abstract; exact message interfaces are not specified here.
matrix_claim_mappings.assumptions: The claim is limited to the publisher abstract's description of the IAC AV-24 racecar experiment; any comparative or performance conclusion depends on the paper's track, vehicle, competition and evaluation protocol.

Direct full-text open returned HTTP 403.

matrix_claim_mappings.claim_limit: Publisher abstract/indexed record only; direct ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403 and full paper was not inspected. Full-scale track validation is not public-road ADS validation, safety certification or proof of robustness across vehicles/ODDs. No detailed lap/performance metric, 100-Hz result or model comparison is asserted from the abstract-only pass.

It is a research alternative to other MPC/controller structures only under comparable vehicle, ODD and interface assumptions; no road-use preference or learning prerequisite follows.

It is a research codebase, not a deployable or road-validated planner.

These are the authors' documented setup, not independently reproduced dependencies.
